Free worry tools

20 short exercises on worry, 2 to 9 minutes each, free and with no account needed. Open one and it runs right in the page.

The 20 tools

  • The worry sorter

    Sort your current worries into ones you can act on, ones you cannot control, and ones you are not sure about yet.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • Where your worry goes

    Divide 100 points across areas of life to show where your worrying attention actually lands.

    Budget · 4 min

  • From "what if" to "what is"

    Take one "what if" that has been circling and walk it through a handful of grounding questions.

    Guided writing · 7 min

  • Your worry habits

    Rate how often a set of common worry patterns has been true for you lately, from seeking reassurance to worrying about worrying.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • Set up a worry window

    Design a short, scheduled slot for worrying on purpose, so the rest of the day has somewhere to send it. An experiment, not a rule.

    Plan builder · 5 min

  • Worry or problem solving?

    Turn over cards that show a worrying thought on one side and the questions that separate worry from real problem solving on the other.

    Perspective cards · 5 min

  • When worry fills the quiet

    Mark the times of day and days of the week when worry tends to move in. Worry has favorite hours, and they are usually the ones with the least to do.

    Week map · 3 min

  • Seven days of worry, weighed

    Each evening, rate how much of the day went to worrying and how useful that worrying turned out to be. By day four the two bars usually stop matching.

    7-day log · 2 min

  • The fears under your worries

    Worries change from week to week, but the fears underneath them tend to repeat. Choose the ones you recognize and put them in the order they come up.

    Card pick · 5 min

  • How your worry behaves, on seven dials

    Set a dial for each way worry can operate: how easily it starts, how long it runs, how believable it sounds, how much it steers you. The pattern across the dials is the point.

    Dials · 4 min

  • The tells that give worry away

    Tick the small signs, in your body and your behavior, that show you are worrying before you have noticed you are. Catching worry by its tells is easier than catching it by its thoughts.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • Shelve it for now

    A short, timed way to set one worry down on purpose without pretending it is gone: write it in a line, name when you will come back to it, and give your attention to something else for three minutes.

    Guided exercise · 6 min

  • Count the breath, not the worry

    Four in, a two-second pause, six out, eight times. Counting gives a worried mind a small, boring job to do, and a worried body a slower rhythm to follow.

    Breathing · 2 min

  • Whose worry is it

    Place your current worries on a grid of how much they are yours to carry against how much thought they get. The corner to look at is where things that are not yours get most of your attention.

    Grid · 6 min

  • What actually settles a worry

    Rank the things that make a worry quieter, for you specifically, from most reliable to least. Most people discover that what they reach for and what works are two different lists.

    Ranking · 4 min

  • Past, present, or far ahead

    Sort your worries by when the thing you are worrying about actually sits in time: already over, happening now, or a long way off. Each of the three deserves a different response.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • A worry that actually came true

    Most worries do not come true. Write about one that did, and what happened next. People usually find that the feared thing and the surviving of it were two different sizes.

    Guided writing · 9 min

  • What you believe about worrying

    Rate how much you agree with a set of beliefs people hold about worry itself: that it shows you care, that it keeps bad things away, that it cannot be stopped. Beliefs like these are what keep worry in a job.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • What worry has quietly borrowed

    Choose the things worry has taken from you in the last month, from sleep to a plan you canceled to a good moment you could not quite enjoy. Naming the cost is not self-pity; it is accounting.

    Card pick · 4 min

  • A plan for the 3 a.m. worry

    Decide, in daylight, what you will do when worry wakes you in the middle of the night. A plan made at 3 p.m. is far more use than any decision you make at 3 a.m.

    Plan builder · 6 min

What these tools are, and are not

Every tool here is free and works without an account: choose cards, move dials, sort a list, follow a paced breath, or keep a seven-day log, and read back what you noticed at the end. They are built to make a vague feeling more specific, which is often the first useful step.

None of them diagnoses, screens for or treats anything, and nothing you see at the end is a score or a label. If something you notice worries you, a licensed therapist is the right next conversation, and the directory is free to browse.
